To show support for our new power efficiency benchmarks, grab a LIMITED Disappointment PC T-Shirt on the GN store! https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/disappointment-pc-2023-heather in Charcoal Heather!
This review & benchmark looks at the NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super graphics card that just launched. This also fully refreshes our dataset for 2024 video card benchmark charts, with the exception of the RTX 4060 that we're running through now to join the upcoming AMD RX 7600 XT GPU review for its launch. The RTX 4070 Ti Super gets the most direct comparisons vs. the RTX 4070 Ti and RTX 4070 Super, but the 4070 Ti (original) will be discontinued. The next GPU launch from NVIDIA is the RTX 4080 Super, which we suspect will be the most interesting for most people. As for AMD alternatives, the AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT remains the most price competitive in the class of the 4070 Ti Super (which has an MSRP of $800). Tests will look at power efficiency, ray tracing (we just added Cyberpunk!), and standard rasterized gaming benchmarks. Resolutions include 1080p, 1440p, and 4K.

comments.text:
More cuda cores will always make the GPU more power efficient. In other words the higher the graphic card class is the more efficient it is as you can clock it lower and have a higher FPS at the same power of lower class cards. When we talk about efficiency then we are targeting the audience that think power does matter and these people are more likely to undervolt their cards and use them at a lower power level.

At this point, showing off efficiency at stock speeds which mostly already past the efficient boost is not very meaningful for that kind of audience. The efficiency testing should include an efficiency curve that goes from   base level voltage to the highest power the GPU can use. However this kind of testing can be a lot difficult since every game will have a different FPS per watt at a certain power stage of the tested GPU, and I guess that you guys are not old enough to do such a thing 😅. However.... the efficiency curve testing can be done on a 1 certain benchmark that you guys think it is enough to represent the efficiency comparison very well between the tested GPUs.

comments.text:
As a reminder why Frames/Watt is important - every Watt of power (really every Joule) your components need to generate, MUST be dissipated out of your system somehow or you'll have components generating errors, thermal throttling, shutting down, or failing.  Basic thermodynamics.  Not to mention getting better performance at lower wattages means less power used - which typically means less money spent paying for that power.  

Now I'll say that GN needs to do further commentary on this metric.  Because you can't just look at the number by itself.  A card may be very power efficient, but not perform competitively.  So there are several axes that need to be considered.  Time for 3D graphs!  :P

comments.text:
This review brings to mind something I've been wondering for a while now (although this particular product doesn't have this issue, it shows that others do): why don't memory manufacturers make 1.5GB/12Gb VRAM packages? AFAIK there's no technical reason why we only have 1GB and 2GB packages (but if there is, I'd love to learn!), and with current memory bus widths and capacities this makes product segmentation SO weird and problematic, with the 16GB 4060 Ti being perhaps the most emblematic of this for the current generation. Put simply: the 1x/2x scaling of current VRAM makes for huge jumps between capacities on the same VRAM bus (8 or 16GB, 12 or 24GB, etc.), which raises costs for higher memory SKUs, messes up product segmentation and doesn't bring any tangible benefit to consumers.

Yes, I get that memory makers would much rather sell 8 2GB chips than 8 slightly cheaper 1.5GB chips, but what that often results in is them selling 8 1GB chips instead, which ... kind of sucks for everyone involved.

If we had 1.5GB VRAM packages, we could have a 12GB 4060 Ti with no other changes, which would make much more sense than both the 8GB and 16GB models. If we had 1.5GB VRAM packages, the 10GB RTX 3080 could have had 15GB of VRAM, and it would have been far more viable long-term (without the cost of going to 20GB, which it doesn't need). It would allow any 128-bit bus card to have either 8, 12 or 16GB of VRAM, any 192-bit bus card 12, 18 or 24, and so on. And, of course, it would allow GPU makers more freedom in setting bus widths for cards according to what they actually might have use for, rather than the current situation where it's often clear that a card gets X bus width because Y bus width would raise the base price for an acceptable amount of memory too much (i.e. upper midrange cards stuck with 192-bit bus widths because 256-bit would force 16GB of VRAM as a base acceptable spec (8GB being far too little for that product tier) on top of the increase in board cost, when 1.5GB chips would allow for 256-bit buses and still 12GB of VRAM, which would perform better in a lot of scenarios.

comments.text:
Power efficiency and pricing has to do with node - TSMC makes nearly everything.

* RTX 40 - TSMC 4nm
* RX 7000 - TSMC 5nm/6nm
* RX 6000 - TSMC 6nm/7nm
* Intel Arc - TSMC 6nm 

When a node is new, it's more expensive. RTX 40 used the absolute newest node available, hence it was expensive. Now that the node matured, they can release cheaper products. 

AMD will use TSMC 4nm for Phoenix APUs (7040 mobile, 8000G desktop) which they designed ages ago, and are just now releasing as the price is getting cheaper. 

Nvidia is moving into the AI space - so using a bleeding edge node means their cards will be the most efficient and cutting edge, but that it will come at a cost premium at first.

AMD isn't in the AI space nearly as much, so they wait for old nodes to come down in price. 

Before AI, Nvidia used maturer nodes which allowed for cheaper products.

Given that for higher FPS we need higher boost frequencies and those don't scale anywhere near "linearly" regarding power consumption X work delivered, I think those "uncapped FPS efficiencies" may differ significantly from the efficiency the card would deliver at what I would call "reasonable playing conditions".
Like, even if I purchase a 4090, I would still play a whole lot of games that wouldn't get even close to maxing out their capabilities (unless I wanted to waste money on extra frames to be discarted before they even get to the monitor), so most of the time it would be running at a different scale of "efficiency" than it's maxxed out one.

I realize though that would mean even more work on your already really well made and thought out reviews, for perhaps a not-so-exceptional return in terms of data, so I'm not keeping high hopes, but one can dream, right?

This being my first AMD card, I'm pretty blown away. It does require more tuning than the plug-and-play Nvidia cards I'm used to (coming from a 3060), but once everything is dialed in this card is buttery smooth. I was especially blown away by its performance in VR applications. I went from getting around 40fps in Assetto Corsa to a stable 75ish with enhanced graphics.

Many people diss on AMD for their ray tracing capabilities, and while I have to admit that I don't think their algorithm is as pretty as Nvidia's, it definitely at least holds up and is good enough that I'm not hurting for better, especially when taken into consideration the price difference and the fact that it is likely to be expanded on in future driver updates. 

All in all, after doing a lot of research, I think the 7900 XT 20GB is the best bang for the buck in the ~$800 GPU range rn.

comments.text: ​ @Aquaquake keep in mind that there is a node difference between AMD and Nvidia, which means that for peak clock speeds AMD will be spending much more power to get the top end. Nvidia's dies are also monolithic so they are going to be slightly more efficient from that. Final piece of the puzzle is Nvidia has RT hardware acceleration which makes computing RT tasks more energy efficient than AMD's methods (right now, they will probably add hardware acceleration too next generation or the gen after). Mix that together and you see that ~20-30% efficiency lead. Honestly I am surprised it's not more but sdram isn't scaling well with node shrinks so maybe that's it

comments.text:
@milkgxng  And? My last build was in 2015 or so. Still going strong on an i7 4785T and GTX 970, and only now with Baldur's Gate 3 do I have any serious wish for a more powerful machine. ...which would be either a 5800X3D system, or more wisely in a few years a 7800X3D system, possibly sticking with the same GPU for a while. And even then, I'd probably run that in Eco Mode, because I only have a 1920x1200 monitor.

My machine before that, built from 2009 tech? My mother still uses it for Facebook and banking stuff, with a GT 430 stuck in it for hardware video decode. She's happy with everything but the WiFi dongle's reception, which is unrelated. That PSU is still in good shape, too.

PSU's are the single most reusable part of a build... only if they a) fail, which shouldn't happen if you're not making the LITERAL WORST choice of components to skimp on quality of, or are majorly overloading, or b) can't output the load needed by Intel and GPU manufacturer's obsession with chasing clockspeed over reasonable efficiency for years.

A properly chosen ATX PSU can be used for well over 10 years, and even then at that point if a load-tester finds the output to still be in spec? It's STILL usable. So that power efficiency leads to free money, if you're not selling off the entire machine to pay for a new spaceheater I mean uber-gaming-rig.

So yes, the ROI is many years, but I broke even years ago, and I'm still going -- and since the PC component market is batshit insane price-wise and energy consumption wise, I'll keep going. :)

Others can do the same. Honestly, it's more interesting to squeeze performance out of a lower-end-but-not-cheaped-out build, and past a certain point there is a sharply diminshing rate of return of quality-per-dollar anyway.

comments.text: Including idle and life cycle of the device is massively complex and can't reasonably be done without too many assumptions. That said, we can do cost calculation approximations based on an assumed amount of hours gaming per day. The trouble is that it'll be at different frame rates, so naturally higher-performing cards will "cost" more to run and may not be directly comparable. To have a true like-for-like, you'd probably need to FPS-normalize or something. Otherwise, it would amount to "better card cost more" basically. We did some exploration into this in our CPU efficiency testing, if you're curious.
